dct_description_sm: This collection of archival sources was generated to fulfill two key goals of the project: 1) to create an archival evidence base to assess the social, environmental, and economic impact of mineral development of the Polaris lead-zinc mine, Little Cornwallis Island, in the Inuit community of Resolute; 2) to assess and analyze the historical memories of communities in relation to large scale industrialization and de-industrialization associated with large scale mineral projects.  The Polaris lead-zinc mine was operated by Cominco on Little Cornwallis Island from 1982-2002 as one of the first long distance commuting mines in the former Northwest Territories, and one of the very few historical large-scale historical mining projects in present-day Nunavut. Researchers collected documentary evidence from four different archives to assess the historical role of the federal government and the mining company Cominco as promoters of the Polaris Mine. Archival evidence was also assembled to analyze the role of the Canadian Arctic Resources Committee (CARC) as a lobbyist on environmental and social concerns about the mine. The archival evidence was assembled as a complement to oral history interviews that captured local Inuit attitudes toward Polaris Mine (see separate PDC entry).
